answer: So TCP handles this using AIMD—additive increase, multiplicative decrease. Basically, it starts off in slow start to quickly see how much bandwidth is available, and then in congestion avoidance, it gradually increases the window size line by line to get maximum throughput. If it detects packet loss—like through repeated ACKs or a timeout—it immediately cuts the window size way down, like halving it or dropping back to one segment. That way it backs off quickly before the whole network gets overwhelmed.

author: ninad
answer: BFS basically explores a graph level by level using a queue. You start at a node, visit all of its immediate neighbors first—so everything at distance 1—and then move on to their neighbors at distance 2, and so on. Because it expands outward in layers, you're guaranteed to visit nodes in order of how far they are from the start, which is super handy for finding shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

key_points: BFS explores all neighbour nodes in the first level before moving to the next level.

We usually prefer composition because it gives you way more flexibility. With inheritance, you're tightly coupled to the parent class at compile time, but with composition, you can swap out behavior dynamically at runtime just by changing the underlying component. It keeps things loosely coupled and much easier to test.

author: nandu
answer: Horspool's algorithm builds a single shift table, for which each charecter in the pattern except the last, the shift is the distance from its rightmost occurrence to the end of the pattern.Every other charecter gets a shift equal to the pattern length m. It always compares from right to left during matching, but on a mismatch it will always shift according to the text charecter aligned with the last pattern position. Boyer-Moore algorithm builds two tables, one for the bad character rule and one for the good suffix rule. The bad character table is similar to Horspool's shift table, but it includes all characters in the alphabet, not just those in the pattern. The good suffix table allows for larger shifts when a mismatch occurs after a partial match. As a result, Boyer-Moore on the other hand builds 2 tables: a bad character table that uses the mismatched text character and how many text characters have been matched already, and a good suffix table uses the matched suffix to align it with another occurrence of that suffix in the pattern or with a prefix.Both preprocess in O(m + alphabet size), but boyer moore's good suffix table is more complex to build, meanwhile horspool has a lesser overhead and works well on average for large alphabets and natural text bu in worse case is O(nm). The algo then takes the longer of the two shifts.

labelled_on.question: Compare the preprocessing steps of Horspool’s and Boyer-Moore algorithms, and explain how these differences affect their performance in string matching.
key_points: Horspool uses one shift table based on the text character.
Boyer-Moore uses two tables: bad-symbol and good-suffix shifts.

The browser verfies the signature chain, the domain name and the validity dates, which authenticates the server and protects against impersonation. The two sides then run a key exchange, typically ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, to derive a shared session key without ever sending it over the wire.
